option_description: Identifies the transport protocol used to deliver configuration updates to managed components, encompassing both application-layer (e.g., HTTP, MQTT) and transport-layer (e.g., TLS-wrapped gRPC) protocol identity. This single attribute gates the most critical exposure rule: if the protocol is inherently plaintext (http, telnet, snmp_v1, snmp_v2c, ftp, tftp, other_plaintext), a finding is raised immediately regardless of other settings.
security_impact: The Rego policy `unencrypted_update_channel` fires on two paths: (1) directly when the protocol is in the plaintext set [http, telnet, snmp_v1, snmp_v2c, ftp, tftp, other_plaintext], and (2) when the protocol is not plaintext but both mutual_tls_enforced and payload_integrity_verification are false — meaning an 'encrypted' protocol label alone is insufficient. Plaintext protocols expose full configuration payloads, embedded credentials, and secrets to any on-path observer (MITRE T1040 Network Sniffing) and enable exfiltration via unencrypted channels (T1048.003). Additionally, the `update_channel_over_untrusted_network_segment` rule uses this attribute indirectly through transport_encryption_enabled derivation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture live update traffic on the management interface using tcpdump or Wireshark and identify the protocol from packet headers and port numbers.
how_to_obtain.command: sudo tcpdump -i <mgmt_iface> -nn -c 200 'port 80 or port 443 or port 22 or port 161 or port 162 or port 21 or port 69 or port 1883 or port 8883' -w /tmp/update_capture.pcap && tshark -r /tmp/update_capture.pcap -T fields -e frame.protocols | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Protocol stack strings such as 'eth:ethertype:ip:tcp:http', 'eth:ethertype:ip:tcp:tls', 'eth:ethertype:ip:udp:snmp' identifying the exact protocol in use.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the configuration management agent or controller configuration file for the protocol or endpoint URL that specifies how updates are pushed or pulled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'server = https://puppet.example.com:8140', 'chef_server_url https://chef.example.com/organizations/myorg', or 'master: salt.example.com' revealing protocol scheme.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap to probe the update endpoint port and identify the service protocol.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Service version output showing e.g. '443/tcp open ssl/http', '161/udp open snmp', '50051/tcp open grpc' identifying the actual protocol.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the configuration management platform web console, navigate to the agent connection or transport settings page to read the configured protocol.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Puppet Enterprise: Admin > Node Management > Agent Settings > Transport; Ansible Tower/AWX: Settings > Jobs > Isolation; SaltStack Enterprise: Administration > Master Configuration > Transport
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A protocol field showing 'https', 'ssh', 'grpc_tls', or similar indicating the configured update channel transport.

option_description: Indicates whether mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication is fully enforced on the configuration update channel, meaning both the server presents a certificate validated by the client and the client presents a certificate validated by the server. This is a high-level composite flag representing the operational status of mTLS rather than individual configuration knobs.
security_impact: Referenced by three rules. In `unencrypted_update_channel`, when the protocol is not inherently plaintext, absence of mutual_tls_enforced combined with absence of payload_integrity_verification triggers a high-criticality finding. In `unauthenticated_update_source_routing`, absence of mutual_tls_enforced alongside absent BGP route filtering raises a medium finding (T1557.003, T1599). In `missing_mutual_tls_authentication`, this attribute represents the desired end-state; the rule decomposes it into tls_enabled, client_certificate_authentication_required, and client_ca_certificate_configured to find the specific gap. Without mTLS, any host on the network can impersonate the management controller and push malicious configurations (MITRE T1649), and rogue managed components can receive authoritative update payloads.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the TLS configuration of the update server or agent daemon for fields that enable client certificate requirement and CA validation simultaneously.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'ssl_verify_client on; ssl_client_certificate /etc/ssl/ca.crt;' (nginx) or 'tls_client_auth: require' indicating full mTLS enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use openssl s_client to test whether the server requests a client certificate during the TLS handshake.
how_to_obtain.command: echo '' | openssl s_client -connect <update_server>:<port> -tls1_2 2>&1 | grep -E '(Acceptable client certificate|Request CERTIFICATE|Verify return code|Certificate chain)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Acceptable client certificate CA names' list present in output confirms server requests client cert; absence means server-only TLS.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to connect to the update endpoint without a client certificate and observe whether the connection is rejected.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection failure with 'SSL alert: certificate required' or HTTP 400/403 'No required SSL certificate was sent' confirms mTLS enforcement; successful response without cert means mTLS is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the configuration management team to confirm whether mTLS is operationally enforced end-to-end, including any load balancers or proxies that may terminate TLS and re-originate without client certificates.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review network architecture diagrams and ask: 'Does every hop from controller to managed component enforce client certificate validation, including intermediate proxies and load balancers?'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented confirmation that all TLS termination points require and validate client certificates against a trusted CA.

option_description: Indicates whether configuration update payloads are cryptographically signed (e.g., using GPG/PGP detached signatures, HMAC-SHA256, or similar) and whether the receiving component validates the signature before applying any configuration. This operates at the message/payload layer, independent of transport encryption, providing a second integrity layer that survives TLS termination at load balancers or proxies.
security_impact: Used in two rules. In `unencrypted_update_channel`, when the protocol is not plaintext, the rule requires at least one of mutual_tls_enforced or payload_integrity_verification; if both are false, a high-criticality exposure is raised — meaning payload signing can compensate for absent mTLS. In `unauthenticated_update_source_routing`, absence of payload_integrity_verification alongside absent BGP route filtering triggers a finding, because without payload signing, redirected traffic to a rogue distribution point cannot be detected. Without this control, a TLS-terminating MitM (T1562.010 Downgrade Attack) or an intermediate proxy can modify configuration content without the managed component detecting tampering.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect configuration management agent settings for signature verification configuration fields.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'module_authentication: hmac-sha256' (Salt), 'policy_file_mode: 0400' with GPG keyring configured, or 'verify_api_cert: true' with payload signature field confirming signing is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check if the update distribution system (e.g., apt, yum, Puppet, Chef) is configured to validate payload signatures and whether verification failures cause rejection.
how_to_obtain.command: puppet config print | grep -E '(catalog|signature|ssl|certificate)'; salt-call config.get module_dirs; chef-client --config-option verify_api_cert=true --why-run 2>&1 | grep -i 'signature\|integrity\|verify'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output confirming signature verification is active and that unsigned or tampered payloads are rejected rather than applied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review change management documentation and deployment pipeline definitions to confirm whether payload signing is mandated and tested.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request the deployment runbook or CI/CD pipeline configuration (e.g., Jenkinsfile, GitLab CI YAML, GitHub Actions workflow) and look for signing steps and signature verification gates before configuration is applied.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pipeline stages showing 'gpg --verify', 'sha256sum --check', or equivalent verification steps that fail-fast if signature validation fails.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review agent or configuration management logs for evidence of signature verification events.
how_to_obtain.command: journalctl -u puppet -u chef-client -u salt-minion --since '7 days ago' | grep -iE '(signature|integrity|verify|checksum|tamper|invalid)' | tail -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries such as 'Catalog signature verified successfully' or 'Signature verification failed, rejecting payload' confirming the feature is active.

option_description: Indicates whether TLS encryption is enabled at all on the update or management channel between the configuration controller and managed components. This is the foundational prerequisite for any TLS-based security property; without it, all subsequent mTLS and cipher controls are moot. It captures the binary state of whether the channel is encrypted at the transport layer regardless of TLS version or cipher quality.
security_impact: The `missing_mutual_tls_authentication` rule fires on three distinct conditions, the first being: `not input.tls_enabled`. If TLS is not enabled at all, the exposure is raised immediately without evaluating client certificate or CA settings. A channel without TLS transmits all configuration payloads, authentication tokens, and management commands in cleartext, enabling any on-path attacker to read, record, and replay update traffic (MITRE T1649, T1556.001). This attribute also logically underpins the `update_channel_protocol` assessment — a protocol value of 'https' with tls_enabled=false would represent a misconfiguration where TLS has been disabled despite the endpoint being labeled HTTPS.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a TLS handshake directly against the update endpoint port to confirm whether TLS is active.
how_to_obtain.command: echo 'Q' | openssl s_client -connect <update_server>:<port> -timeout 5 2>&1 | head -20 | grep -E '(CONNECTED|SSL-Session|verify|no peer certificate|errno)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'CONNECTED' followed by certificate chain details and 'SSL-Session' block confirms TLS is enabled; 'errno' or immediate close without SSL negotiation confirms TLS is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect daemon or server configuration files for TLS enable/disable flags.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'tls_enabled: true' or 'ssl on;' confirms TLS is active; 'tls_enabled: false', 'insecure: true', or 'ssl off;' confirms it is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap with SSL scripts to detect TLS on the update channel port.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ssl-cert' script output with certificate details confirms TLS is enabled; port shown as 'open' without ssl script output or labeled as 'unencrypted' confirms TLS is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the configuration management platform's admin console and inspect the agent communication or transport security settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Puppet Enterprise: Admin > Infrastructure > Puppet Infrastructure Settings > Communications; Ansible AWX: Settings > System > Enable/Disable TLS; Chef Infra: Administration > Organizations > Settings > SSL
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 'TLS Enabled' or 'SSL Required' toggle set to enabled/on, or an endpoint URL beginning with 'https://' or 'grpcs://'.

option_description: Indicates whether the update channel's TLS server is configured to require managed component clients to present a valid X.509 certificate during the TLS handshake. This enforces the client-authentication half of mutual TLS, preventing anonymous or unauthenticated clients from establishing connections to the update distribution endpoint.
security_impact: The `missing_mutual_tls_authentication` rule's second condition fires when `tls_enabled == true` but `not input.client_certificate_authentication_required`. Server-only TLS encrypts the channel but provides no assurance about the client's identity, allowing any host that can reach the endpoint to receive update payloads. Combined with absent client CA validation, this means a rogue managed component could obtain configuration updates intended for legitimate components, or an attacker could impersonate a managed component to receive sensitive configuration data. MITRE T1649 (Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates) is the primary exploitation path, as forged client certificates cannot be detected without this control enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the TLS server configuration for client authentication mode settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ssl_verify_client on;' (nginx), 'SSLVerifyClient require' (Apache), 'verify required' (HAProxy), or 'ClientAuth: RequireAndVerifyClientCert' confirms client certificate authentication is required.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Connect to the update endpoint without providing a client certificate and observe whether the handshake succeeds or fails.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TLS alert 'certificate required' (alert code 116) or HTTP 400 'No required SSL certificate was sent' confirms client certificate is required; a successful 200 response confirms it is not required.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use openssl s_client to inspect the TLS handshake for a Certificate Request message from the server.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl s_client -connect <update_server>:<port> -key /dev/null -cert /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E '(Acceptable client certificate CA names|Request CERTIFICATE|no client certificate|Certificate chain|handshake failure)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'Acceptable client certificate CA names' section with CA DN entries confirms the server requests a client certificate.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the configuration management API or service mesh control plane for the authentication policy applied to the update endpoint.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get destinationrule -n <mgmt-namespace> -o yaml | grep -A5 'tls:'; istioctl proxy-config listener <update-server-pod> | grep -i 'client_cert'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'mode: MUTUAL' in the DestinationRule TLS section, or 'require_client_certificate: true' in the Envoy listener config confirms client certificate authentication is required.

option_description: Indicates whether a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) certificate or bundle is configured on the update channel server for validating client certificates presented during mTLS handshakes. Even if client certificate authentication is nominally required, without a CA bundle the server cannot verify the client certificate's chain of trust, rendering the requirement operationally ineffective and potentially allowing any self-signed certificate to be accepted.
security_impact: The `missing_mutual_tls_authentication` rule's third and most specific condition fires when `tls_enabled == true AND client_certificate_authentication_required == true AND not input.client_ca_certificate_configured`. This condition catches deployments that have correctly enabled TLS and required client certificates but failed to configure the CA trust anchor — a subtle misconfiguration that defeats the purpose of mTLS. Without a trusted CA bundle, the server cannot distinguish between a certificate issued by the legitimate organizational CA and one self-signed by an attacker, enabling MITRE T1649 certificate forgery to succeed even with mTLS nominally enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the TLS server configuration for a client CA certificate file or directory path.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ssl_client_certificate /etc/ssl/client-ca.crt;' (nginx), 'SSLCACertificateFile /etc/apache2/ssl/ca.crt' (Apache), or 'client_ca_file: /opt/pki/ca.pem' confirms a CA certificate is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that the CA certificate file referenced in configuration actually exists, is readable, and contains valid certificate content.
how_to_obtain.command: CA_FILE=$(grep -rEi 'ssl_client_certificate|client_ca_file|SSLCACertificateFile' /etc/nginx/ /etc/apache2/ /opt/mgmt-server/ 2>/dev/null | awk -F'[= ]+' '{print $NF}' | tr -d '"' | head -1); [ -n "$CA_FILE" ] && openssl x509 -in "$CA_FILE" -noout -subject -issuer -dates 2>&1 || echo 'CA file not found or not configured'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Certificate subject, issuer, and validity dates output confirms CA file exists and is valid PEM. 'CA file not found' confirms the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For gRPC or Go-based update agents, check for CA certificate configuration in daemon flags or environment variables.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep -E '(grpc|mgmt-agent|update-daemon)' | grep -oE '(--ca-cert|--tls-ca|--client-ca|CA_CERT_FILE)[= ][^ ]+'; systemctl cat <mgmt-agent>.service | grep -E '(CA|ca_cert|client_ca)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: '--ca-cert=/opt/pki/ca.pem' or 'CA_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/ca-bundle.crt' in process flags confirms CA certificate is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes-based deployments, check the Secret or ConfigMap providing the CA certificate to the update service pod.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get secret -n <mgmt-namespace> | grep -i 'ca\|tls'; kubectl describe secret <tls-secret-name> -n <mgmt-namespace> | grep -E '(ca\.crt|ca-bundle)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secret containing 'ca.crt' key with non-empty data confirms a CA certificate is mounted and available to the update service.

option_description: Specifies the lowest TLS protocol version that the update channel server or client will accept during negotiation. Setting a permissive minimum allows downgrade attacks where an attacker forces negotiation to a weaker protocol version with known cryptographic vulnerabilities, even if newer versions are also supported.
security_impact: The `weak_or_deprecated_tls_ciphers` rule fires when `input.minimum_tls_version in ["SSLv2", "SSLv3", "TLSv1.0", "TLSv1.1"]`. SSLv2 and SSLv3 have fundamental design flaws (POODLE, DROWN); TLSv1.0 and TLSv1.1 use SHA-1 and have known weaknesses enabling BEAST and other attacks. Allowing these versions enables MITRE T1600 (Weaken Encryption) and T1600.001 (Reduce Key Space) attacks where an active MitM can force downgrade to a version where decryption or forgery of configuration payloads becomes computationally feasible. Industry and regulatory standards (PCI DSS, NIST SP 800-52r2) require a minimum of TLSv1.2, with TLSv1.3 recommended.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use testssl.sh to enumerate all accepted TLS versions on the update endpoint and identify the minimum version accepted.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'SSLv3 not offered', 'TLSv1 not offered', 'TLSv1.1 not offered', 'TLSv1.2 offered', 'TLSv1.3 offered (OK)' showing the minimum accepted version.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap ssl-enum-ciphers script to detect accepted TLS versions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Script output listing TLS versions as 'TLSv1.2: ciphers: ...' with older versions absent, or present if insecurely configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect TLS configuration files for minimum version directives across common web servers and management daemons.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;' (nginx) or 'SSLProtocol all -SSLv3 -TLSv1 -TLSv1.1' (Apache) or 'min_tls_version: TLSv1.2' showing the enforced minimum.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt explicit connection using deprecated TLS versions to confirm they are rejected.
how_to_obtain.command: for ver in ssl2 ssl3 tls1 tls1_1; do echo -n "$ver: "; echo 'Q' | openssl s_client -connect <update_server>:<port> -$ver 2>&1 | grep -oE '(CONNECTED|handshake failure|no protocols|alert|unknown)' | head -1; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'handshake failure' or 'no protocols available' for ssl2, ssl3, tls1, tls1_1 confirms those versions are rejected; 'CONNECTED' for any deprecated version confirms the minimum is too low.

option_description: Enumerates the specific TLS cipher suites that the update channel server and client are configured to negotiate or accept. Individual cipher suites determine the key exchange algorithm, bulk encryption algorithm, and MAC function used to protect update traffic. The presence of any weak cipher (RC4, 3DES, NULL, EXPORT, aNULL, DES) in the allowed list constitutes a security risk even if strong ciphers are also present, because a downgrade attack can force selection of the weakest mutually supported option.
security_impact: The `weak_or_deprecated_tls_ciphers` rule checks each weak cipher suite individually: if any of RC4, 3DES, EXPORT, NULL, aNULL, or DES appear in `input.allowed_cipher_suites`, the rule fires. This is additive to the minimum TLS version check — a system running TLSv1.2 with RC4 ciphers is still flagged. Weak ciphers directly enable MITRE T1600 (Weaken Encryption) as RC4 has well-documented biases enabling statistical plaintext recovery, 3DES is vulnerable to SWEET32 birthday attacks, EXPORT ciphers use 40/56-bit keys breakable by nation-state actors, and NULL/aNULL ciphers provide no encryption at all. For configuration update channels specifically, decryption of a single session may reveal infrastructure topology, credentials, or allow injection of malicious configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run testssl.sh against the update endpoint to enumerate all accepted cipher suites and flag weak ones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines flagging weak ciphers such as 'RC4 (Attention! Vulnerable cipher)' or 'DES-CBC3-SHA' with VULNERABLE or WEAK rating. Clean output with only ECDHE/AES-GCM/ChaCha20 suites indicates secure configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap ssl-enum-ciphers to get a graded cipher list for the update endpoint.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cipher entries graded 'F' (NULL/EXPORT/RC4) or 'D' (weak) indicate critical issues. Only 'A' grade ciphers (ECDHE-*-AES*-GCM) indicates secure configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect TLS configuration files for cipher suite directives and identify any weak entries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'ssl_ciphers ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384;' is secure. Presence of 'RC4', '3DES', 'DES', 'EXPORT', 'NULL', or 'aNULL' in the cipher string is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Go-based agents or gRPC services, extract the cipher suite configuration from the binary or environment.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cipher suite names extracted from the binary; presence of 'TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128' or 'TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA' constants indicates weak ciphers are compiled in or configured.

option_description: Controls what per-message freshness mechanism is applied to configuration update payloads to prevent replay attacks. Options include cryptographic nonces, monotonic sequence numbers, bounded timestamps, or no protection.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires replay_of_configuration_update_messages when this value is 'none', and also when a non-none mechanism is selected but update_deduplication_enforced is false. Without replay protection, a captured legitimate update message can be retransmitted by an attacker to revert a component to a previously vulnerable or misconfigured state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect message broker or middleware configuration for replay protection headers or message attributes. For gRPC services, check the service descriptor or interceptor chain.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: References to nonce fields, sequence number tracking, or timestamp window enforcement in service configuration files.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the update channel protocol specification file or message schema definition for freshness field declarations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Schema includes a 'nonce', 'seq_no', or 'issued_at' field with enforcement annotations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the management API to retrieve the update channel configuration and inspect replay protection settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response field replay_protection containing 'nonce', 'sequence_number', or 'timestamp_with_window'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform engineering team responsible for the configuration update pipeline to confirm whether freshness enforcement is part of the message contract.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented evidence that a specific replay protection mechanism is implemented and enforced by receivers.

option_description: Controls whether configuration update messages carry a cryptographic signature or MAC that receivers validate before applying the update. Covers HMAC-based and asymmetric signature schemes.
security_impact: Referenced by the replay_of_configuration_update_messages rule. When false, a captured update message can be tampered with or replayed because the receiver has no cryptographic means to detect modification. The Rego policy also relies on this attribute in combination with replay_protection_mechanism to determine full replay risk exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check gRPC service configuration or REST API gateway settings for signature validation interceptors or middleware.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entries showing HMAC or signature verification is enabled for inbound update messages.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the message queue consumer configuration (e.g., RabbitMQ, Kafka, NATS) for message authentication settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Properties such as 'message.integrity.check=true' or reference to a signature validation plugin.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Call the update service health or capabilities endpoint to determine if message authentication is advertised.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Field message_authentication returns true or lists the supported algorithm (e.g., HS256, RS256).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review update agent logs for signature validation events to determine whether verification is active.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries confirming 'signature verified' or 'HMAC valid' for processed update messages.

option_description: Controls whether the receiving component maintains persistent state to detect and reject duplicate or out-of-order configuration update messages, such as a seen-nonces cache or a last-applied sequence number register.
security_impact: The Rego replay_of_configuration_update_messages rule fires when a non-none replay_protection_mechanism is configured but update_deduplication_enforced is false. A replay protection mechanism on the sender side is ineffective if receivers do not track previously processed message identifiers, because the same signed or sequenced message can still be delivered more than once.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search the update agent source configuration or runtime settings for deduplication state management.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entries enabling deduplication cache or last-applied sequence number persistence.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the update agent configuration file for deduplication or idempotency settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Settings such as 'deduplication_enabled: true' or 'nonce_cache_size: 1000' present in the file.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the update agent runtime API to retrieve deduplication state information.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response contains deduplication enabled flag and optionally the last-seen sequence number or nonce cache statistics.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check update agent logs for duplicate rejection events to confirm deduplication logic is active.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing duplicate update messages being detected and rejected by the agent.

option_description: Controls which message-layer integrity mechanism protects configuration update payloads independently of the transport channel. Options are no protection, HMAC with a shared secret, asymmetric digital signature, or content hash verification.
security_impact: Drives the missing_payload_integrity_verification rule. The Rego policy flags a finding whenever payload_integrity_mechanism is 'none', regardless of whether transport_tls_enforced is true or false, because TLS termination at a proxy or a downgrade attack strips transport protection while leaving payload unverified. Asymmetric signature provides the strongest guarantee as it prevents an insider with only a shared key from forging updates.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the update distribution service or agent configuration for payload signing or hashing directives.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entries specifying a signing algorithm (e.g., RS256, HS512) or content hash algorithm (e.g., SHA-256).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the message schema or API contract for integrity field definitions at the payload layer.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Proto or schema definition includes a 'signature' or 'hmac' field with associated key identifier.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve a sample update payload from the distribution endpoint and inspect it for integrity metadata fields.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Payload response includes a populated signature, hmac, or content_hash field rather than null values.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the update pipeline architecture documentation or interview the engineering team to confirm payload integrity controls are part of the design.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Architecture documentation explicitly states the integrity mechanism used and references key management procedures.

option_description: Controls whether TLS is mandatory and non-negotiable for the configuration update channel, ensuring that no plaintext or downgraded connection can deliver or receive update payloads.
security_impact: Used in the missing_payload_integrity_verification rule. When payload_integrity_mechanism is 'none' and transport_tls_enforced is false, there is no integrity protection at any layer, resulting in a high-severity finding. Even when true, TLS alone is insufficient for payload integrity because TLS termination proxies can inspect and modify payload content before re-encryption.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check service configuration for TLS enforcement flags and confirm the absence of insecure skip flags.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: tls_required set to true and insecure_skip_tls absent or set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a plaintext connection to the update service endpoint to confirm it refuses non-TLS connections.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused or HTTP 301/400 redirect to HTTPS, confirming plaintext connections are rejected.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the update service or API gateway configuration file for TLS enforcement directives.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration contains 'ssl on', 'listen 443 ssl', and no plain 'listen 80' without redirect, or equivalent for the service type.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check load balancer or service mesh configuration via management API to confirm TLS policy enforcement.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get destinationrule update-service -n management -o jsonpath='{.spec.trafficPolicy.tls}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TLS mode is ISTIO_MUTUAL or SIMPLE, confirming transport encryption is enforced at the service mesh layer.

option_description: Controls whether BGP prefix-list or route-map policies are applied to peering sessions on routers handling update traffic, preventing acceptance of more-specific route advertisements that could hijack update traffic to rogue distribution points.
security_impact: Referenced by the unauthenticated_update_source_routing rule. The Rego policy fires when bgp_route_filtering_enabled is false in combination with missing IP allowlists, missing payload integrity verification, or missing mutual TLS. A BGP hijack redirecting update traffic to an attacker-controlled server is a high-impact supply chain attack vector.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Connect to the border or peering router and review BGP neighbor configuration for prefix-list or route-map policies.
how_to_obtain.command: ssh admin@border-router 'show ip bgp neighbor | include prefix-list|route-map|filter-list'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each BGP neighbor session shows inbound and outbound prefix-list or route-map assignments.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the router configuration file for prefix-list definitions and their application to BGP peers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration contains 'neighbor X.X.X.X prefix-list FILTER in' directives for all peering sessions relevant to update traffic paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use FRR or Cisco IOS show commands to verify active route filters on BGP peering sessions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows 'Inbound path policy configured' and lists the active prefix-list or route-map name.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log into the network management platform (e.g., Cisco DNA Center, Juniper APSTRA) and review BGP policy assignments for each peering session.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Network Management Platform > Routing > BGP > Peers > Select peer > Policy tab > Verify Inbound Prefix Filter
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An inbound prefix filter policy is listed and active for each relevant BGP peer session.

option_description: Controls whether managed components maintain a static allowlist of permitted IP addresses for update server connections, blocking connections to any IP not on the list even if routing is manipulated via BGP hijack or DHCP spoofing.
security_impact: Used in the unauthenticated_update_source_routing rule. The Rego policy flags a finding when both bgp_route_filtering_enabled and update_server_ip_allowlist_enforced are false, as the absence of both controls means an attacker can redirect update traffic without any network-layer barrier. The allowlist acts as a defense-in-depth control independent of routing infrastructure integrity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check host-based firewall rules on managed components for outbound IP allowlist enforcement toward update servers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Explicit ACCEPT rules for specific update server IP addresses followed by a DROP default policy for unlisted destinations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the update agent configuration for hardcoded or configurable server IP allowlist settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: File contains a list of permitted update server IP addresses or CIDR ranges with no wildcard entries.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect nftables rules or ufw configuration for update channel outbound destination restrictions.
how_to_obtain.command: nft list ruleset | grep -A3 'update' ; ufw status verbose | grep -E '(update|8443|8080)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules limiting outbound update channel connections to specific IP addresses with explicit deny-all for unmatched destinations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query a configuration management API or endpoint management system for the update server allowlist policy.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response contains a non-empty array of permitted update server IP addresses or CIDR blocks.

option_description: Controls whether request-rate or bandwidth limits are enforced on the configuration update channel endpoints, protecting the management plane from flooding attacks that could exhaust processing capacity or cause denial of service.
security_impact: Drives the absence_of_rate_limiting_on_update_channel rule. The Rego policy fires when rate_limiting_enabled is false and the update channel exposure is public or internal_unrestricted, or when no connection limit is configured regardless of exposure level. Without rate limiting, a compromised component or external attacker can flood the management plane with spurious update requests, disrupting legitimate configuration operations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the API gateway or reverse proxy configuration for rate limiting directives on update channel endpoints.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rate limiting directives such as 'limit_req zone=update burst=10' or equivalent present for update channel location blocks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the API gateway or load balancer configuration for rate limiting policies on management plane endpoints.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration contains limit_req_zone definitions and limit_req directives applied to update endpoint location blocks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the API management console (e.g., Kong Manager, AWS API Gateway, Azure APIM) and verify rate limiting policies on the update endpoint.
how_to_obtain.navigation: API Gateway Console > APIs > Update Service > Policies > Rate Limiting > Verify requests-per-second and burst limits are configured
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rate limiting policy shows a non-zero requests-per-second limit applied to the configuration update endpoint.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the management API or service mesh control plane for rate limiting policy definitions on the update service.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get envoyfilter update-ratelimit -n management -o jsonpath='{.spec.configPatches[*].patch.value}' 2>/dev/null || kubectl get ratelimitpolicy -n management -o yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rate limit policy definition showing per-client or global request limits applied to the update service routes.

option_description: Controls whether a maximum concurrent connection or request concurrency limit is enforced on the configuration update channel listener, acting as a secondary flood-prevention mechanism to cap resource exhaustion from excessive simultaneous connections.
security_impact: The Rego policy for absence_of_rate_limiting_on_update_channel fires when both rate_limiting_enabled is false AND connection_limit_configured is false across all exposure levels including management_network_only. Without this control, a compromised component or attacker can flood the update channel with concurrent connections, exhausting file descriptors, thread pools, or memory on the management controller and causing denial of service to the entire management plane (T1499.002, T1498).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the management API gateway or reverse proxy (e.g., nginx, HAProxy, Envoy) for active connection limit settings on the update channel listener.
how_to_obtain.command: nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'worker_connections|limit_conn|limit_req' ; haproxy -vv 2>/dev/null | grep -i maxconn ; kubectl get configmap -n management -o yaml 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'max.conn|maxConnections|concurrentRequests'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing numeric values for worker_connections, limit_conn_zone, maxconn, or equivalent; absence of these indicates no limit is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the configuration management agent config file (e.g., Puppet agent, Chef client, Ansible pull, or Salt minion) and any fronting proxy configuration for max connection parameters.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Parameters such as 'max_connections', 'maxconn', 'limit_conn', or 'worker_connections' present with a defined integer value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the management controller's admin API for current rate and connection limit configuration on the update endpoint.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing fields like 'max_concurrent_connections' or 'request_concurrency_limit' with non-null integer values.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use a load testing tool to attempt a high volume of concurrent connections to the update channel endpoint and observe whether connections are rejected or queued beyond a threshold.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Failed requests should appear once the connection limit is hit; zero failed requests across 200 concurrent connections indicates no limit is enforced.

option_description: Controls whether the managed component performs full X.509 certificate chain-of-trust validation against a trusted CA bundle when establishing a TLS connection to the management controller, explicitly rejecting self-signed certificates and certificates issued by untrusted or unknown CAs.
security_impact: The Rego policy certificate_validation_bypass_on_managed_component triggers directly when ca_chain_validation_enforced is false, and also when pinned_certificate_or_ca_configured is false AND ca_chain_validation_enforced is false. Without CA chain validation, an attacker performing a man-in-the-middle attack can present any self-signed or rogue CA-signed certificate to substitute a fraudulent update server (T1553.004, T1649, T1608.003), allowing arbitrary malicious configurations to be pushed to managed components.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the managed component's TLS/SSL configuration for the verify_ssl, ssl_verify, tls_ca_cert, or equivalent option that references a trusted CA bundle.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Fields such as 'ssl_verify = true', 'verify_ssl: true', 'ca_file: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.crt', or 'ssl_ca_cert' pointing to a non-empty CA bundle file.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the TLS client configuration of the configuration management agent process for CA validation flags, inspecting running process environment and loaded libraries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No matches for InsecureSkipVerify=true, verify_ssl=false, or check_hostname=False; presence of ca_cert or ca_bundle pointing to a valid file.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a TLS connection to the management controller using a self-signed certificate and observe whether the managed component's agent rejects or accepts it.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl s_client -connect <mgmt-controller>:<port> -CAfile /dev/null -verify_return_error 2>&1 | grep -E 'Verify return|certificate verify failed|OK'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'certificate verify failed' or 'Verify return code: 18 (self signed certificate)' confirms validation is active; 'Verify return code: 0 (ok)' against a self-signed cert indicates bypass.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the management controller web console, navigate to the managed component's trust configuration settings and verify CA validation is enabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management Console > Managed Components > [Component] > Security Settings > TLS/Certificate Validation > CA Chain Validation: Enabled
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CA Chain Validation toggle is set to 'Enabled' and a CA certificate file path or bundle is populated.

option_description: Controls whether the managed component checks and enforces certificate validity period during TLS handshake with the management controller, rejecting connections when the server certificate has passed its notAfter date.
security_impact: The Rego policy certificate_validation_bypass_on_managed_component triggers independently when certificate_expiry_validation_enforced is false. Accepting expired certificates allows attackers to reuse previously captured or stolen certificates that have since expired to impersonate the management controller (T1649). Combined with absent CA chain validation, this creates a compounding bypass condition where any certificate — expired or self-signed — is accepted, fully undermining TLS authentication of the update source.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search configuration files of the managed component's update agent for flags that disable expiry or hostname checks.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No instances of flags set to true/False that skip certificate checks; configuration should show default secure behavior with no override.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test whether the managed component's agent will connect to an endpoint presenting an intentionally expired certificate.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl s_client -connect <mgmt-controller>:<port> 2>&1 | grep -E 'notAfter|expired|certificate verify failed|Verify return code'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'certificate verify failed' or 'Verify return code: 10 (certificate has expired)' confirms expiry enforcement; acceptance of expired cert indicates bypass.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the managed component's TLS handshake logs or update agent logs for any warnings about expired certificates that were accepted rather than rejected.
how_to_obtain.command: journalctl -u puppet -u salt-minion -u chef-client --since '7 days ago' 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'expired|certificate|ssl|tls|handshake' | tail -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing certificate rejection on expiry; absence of 'accepted expired certificate' or equivalent warning messages.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the team responsible for managing the configuration management agent to confirm whether expiry validation is part of the hardening baseline and whether any exceptions have been granted.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review change management records and security baseline documentation for the managed component image or package.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation confirming certificate expiry validation is required by policy and no exceptions are in effect.

option_description: Controls whether the managed component restricts trust to a specific management controller certificate fingerprint or a narrowly scoped CA certificate rather than the system-wide trust store, preventing acceptance of lookalike certificates issued by other trusted CAs.
security_impact: The Rego policy certificate_validation_bypass_on_managed_component fires when both pinned_certificate_or_ca_configured is false AND ca_chain_validation_enforced is false. Even when standard CA chain validation is enabled, an attacker who can obtain a certificate from any CA trusted by the OS trust store can impersonate the management controller (T1553.004, T1608.003). Certificate pinning closes this gap by ensuring only the legitimate controller's certificate or its specific issuing CA is accepted, preventing substitution attacks using certificates issued by other public CAs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the managed component's agent configuration for explicit certificate fingerprint, pinned CA file, or a restricted trust store path scoped only to the management controller's CA.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 'ca_cert' or equivalent field pointing to a specific CA file (not the system bundle at /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt), or a 'fingerprint' field with a SHA-256 hash of the management controller certificate.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the content of the CA file referenced by the agent to confirm it contains only the management controller's issuing CA, not the full system CA bundle.
how_to_obtain.command: CA_FILE=$(grep -rE 'ca_cert|ca_file|tls_ca_cert' /etc/puppet/ /etc/salt/ /etc/chef/ 2>/dev/null | awk -F= '{print $2}' | tr -d ' ' | head -1); [ -n "$CA_FILE" ] && openssl x509 -in $CA_FILE -noout -subject -issuer -fingerprint || echo 'No pinned CA file found'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing a single certificate with subject matching the internal management CA; multiple certificates or a reference to /etc/ssl/certs/ indicates the full system trust store is used without pinning.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the configuration management system's API for the trust anchor configuration of a specific managed component.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON fields showing 'pinned_ca': '<path-or-pem>' or 'certificate_fingerprint': '<sha256-hash>' with non-null values.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the managed component's certificate configuration in the management console to verify whether pinning is configured.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management Console > Managed Components > [Component] > Security Settings > Certificate Trust > Pinned CA or Certificate Fingerprint field
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A specific CA certificate or SHA-256 fingerprint value is present in the pinning field, not empty or set to 'system default'.

option_description: Classifies the network segment over which configuration update traffic traverses — one of dedicated_oob_management (physically or logically isolated management network), vpn_encapsulated (traffic carried over an authenticated VPN tunnel), flat_shared (shared network with other workload traffic), or untrusted_public (traverses internet or untrusted carrier networks).
security_impact: The Rego policy update_channel_over_untrusted_network_segment triggers when network_segment_type is flat_shared or untrusted_public — both without transport encryption AND with transport encryption but without mutual authentication. Flat or public networks dramatically expand the attacker population that can intercept or inject update traffic (T1040, T1599). Even with TLS, absence of mutual authentication on a shared segment allows rogue hosts on the same VLAN to attempt injection. The combination of network_segment_type with transport_encryption_enabled and mutual_authentication_enforced determines whether the finding fires.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify the network interface and VLAN/subnet used by the managed component for update channel traffic and cross-reference with network topology documentation.
how_to_obtain.command: ip route get <mgmt-controller-ip> 2>/dev/null; ip addr show; cat /etc/network/interfaces 2>/dev/null || ip link show | grep -E 'vlan|bond|mgmt|oob'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing the egress interface and subnet for management controller traffic; a dedicated management VLAN (e.g., VLAN 100, 10.0.0.0/24) indicates dedicated_oob_management; shared subnets with application workloads indicate flat_shared.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review switch/VLAN configuration files, firewall rule sets, and network topology diagrams to determine segment classification.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: VLAN ID and subnet assignments; ACLs or firewall rules restricting the update channel subnet to management hosts only indicate dedicated_oob_management; unrestricted rules or internet-routable prefixes indicate flat_shared or untrusted_public.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the network management system (e.g., Cisco DNAC, SolarWinds, NetBox) to confirm VLAN assignment and segment classification for the management controller and managed component interfaces.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Network Management System > Device Inventory > [Managed Component] > Interface Details > VLAN/Segment Assignment
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Interface is assigned to a management VLAN with no production traffic, or is shown as part of a shared production VLAN.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a traceroute from the managed component to the management controller to observe path hops and identify whether traffic traverses shared routers, internet hops, or VPN gateways.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Single hop or direct layer-2 adjacency suggests dedicated_oob_management; VPN gateway hop suggests vpn_encapsulated; shared core router hops suggest flat_shared; public internet IPs in path indicate untrusted_public.

option_description: Controls whether all configuration update traffic between the management controller and managed components is carried over a transport-layer encrypted channel such as TLS 1.2+, TLS 1.3, or IPsec, preventing cleartext interception of configuration payloads, credentials, and secrets embedded in update messages.
security_impact: The Rego policy update_channel_over_untrusted_network_segment fires first when network_segment_type is flat_shared or untrusted_public AND transport_encryption_enabled is false. A second condition fires even when transport encryption is present but mutual_authentication_enforced is false. Additionally, the unencrypted_update_channel rule fires independently when the protocol is plaintext (HTTP, Telnet, SNMP v1/v2c) or when no mutual TLS and no payload integrity are present (T1040, T1048.003). This attribute is a prerequisite for the majority of update channel security controls.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the configuration management agent configuration for TLS enforcement flags and verify the protocol scheme in use.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Protocol references show 'https://', 'tls_enabled: true', or 'ssl: true'; absence of http://, telnet, or unencrypted SNMP references.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture live update channel traffic during a configuration push cycle and verify all packets are TLS-encapsulated.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i <mgmt-interface> -n host <mgmt-controller-ip> -w /tmp/update-capture.pcap & sleep 30 && kill %1; tshark -r /tmp/update-capture.pcap -Y 'http or telnet or snmp' 2>/dev/null | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero plaintext HTTP, Telnet, or SNMP packets; all traffic to management controller appears as TLS handshake and application data records (port 443, 8443, or configured TLS port).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a plaintext connection to the management controller's update endpoint to verify it is rejected.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused, 301/302 redirect to HTTPS, or 400 Bad Request indicating plaintext is not accepted; successful 200 response over HTTP indicates encryption is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the management controller's listener configuration to confirm TLS is required and plaintext is not offered as a fallback.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Listener configuration shows SSL/TLS certificate and key directives with no plaintext fallback port; 'ssl on', 'redirect_http_to_https', or equivalent present.

option_description: Controls whether both the update source (management controller) and the receiving managed component present and validate certificates during TLS handshake (mutual TLS), preventing unauthorized sources from injecting configurations and preventing rogue components from receiving authoritative update payloads.
security_impact: The Rego policy update_channel_over_untrusted_network_segment fires when network_segment_type is flat_shared or untrusted_public AND transport_encryption_enabled is true but mutual_authentication_enforced is false. Without mutual authentication, any host on the network segment that can reach the management controller port can attempt to push configurations, and any host can claim to be a managed component and receive sensitive update payloads. This also relates to the missing_mutual_tls_authentication rule (T1649, T1556.001) which fires when TLS is present but client certificate authentication is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the management controller server configuration for client certificate requirement (ssl_client_cert, require_client_cert, ssl_verify_client) and the managed component agent for client certificate configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Server-side: 'ssl_verify_client on' (nginx), 'ssl_client_auth required' (Puppet), or 'ssl_client_certificate' directive present. Agent-side: client cert and key paths configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a TLS connection to the management controller's update endpoint without presenting a client certificate and observe whether it is rejected.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'SSL alert number 40' (handshake failure), '400 No required SSL certificate was sent', or '403 Forbidden' confirms client certificate is required; successful 200 response indicates mutual auth is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the management controller's TLS session details to confirm client certificates are being presented and validated during active sessions.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl s_client -connect <mgmt-controller>:<update-port> -cert /dev/null -key /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Request CERTIFICATE|Acceptable client|certificate verify|SSL handshake'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Request CERTIFICATE' or 'Acceptable client certificate CA names' in output confirms server is requesting client certificates.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the management controller's API to retrieve the authentication requirements for the update channel endpoint.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response showing 'mutual_tls': true, 'client_certificate_required': true, or equivalent field confirming bidirectional authentication.

option_description: Indicates whether the update protocol exposes unencrypted metadata to passive network observers — such as TLS Server Name Indication (SNI) fields, unencrypted HTTP Host headers, SNMP community strings, or unencrypted MQTT topic names — even when the payload itself is TLS-encrypted, leaking management plane topology and component identity information.
security_impact: The Rego policy protocol_metadata_leakage fires when protocol_supports_sni_or_plaintext_headers is true AND encrypted_client_hello_enabled is false. Even with full payload encryption, plaintext metadata allows passive observers to map the management plane topology, identify managed component hostnames and update frequencies, and potentially intercept SNMP community strings usable for direct device access (T1040, T1048.003). This reconnaissance data reduces the effort required for targeted attacks against the management infrastructure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture update channel traffic with Wireshark or tcpdump during an active configuration push and inspect for visible plaintext metadata fields.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i <mgmt-interface> -n host <mgmt-controller-ip> -w /tmp/meta-capture.pcap & sleep 60 && kill %1; tshark -r /tmp/meta-capture.pcap -Y 'tls.handshake.extensions_server_name or http.host or snmp.community or mqtt.topic' -T fields -e tls.handshake.extensions_server_name -e http.host -e snmp.community -e mqtt.topic 2>/dev/null | grep -v '^$'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-empty output containing hostnames, community strings, or topic names in plaintext; empty output suggests metadata is not exposed in cleartext.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) or equivalent SNI obfuscation is configured on the TLS stack used by the update channel.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SNI value visible in openssl output confirms plaintext SNI exposure; 'encrypted_client_hello' present in config indicates mitigation is in place.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the update protocol configuration to identify whether SNMP (v1/v2c with community strings), unencrypted MQTT, or plain HTTP is used, and check for any SNI obfuscation configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: MQTT configuration showing 'require_certificate true' and listener on TLS port; SNMP configuration using SNMPv3 only (no community strings); HTTP configuration redirecting all to HTTPS with no Host header leakage path.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review access logs on the management controller to determine whether SNI hostnames or HTTP Host headers from managed components are being logged in cleartext, confirming they traverse the network in the clear.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Absence of plaintext SNI or Host header entries in logs from managed component connections, or confirmation that ECH is suppressing SNI visibility.

option_description: Controls whether TLS Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is configured on the update channel, preventing the server name indication (SNI) from being exposed in plaintext to passive network observers during TLS handshake negotiation.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'protocol_metadata_leakage' exposure when 'protocol_supports_sni_or_plaintext_headers' is true and 'encrypted_client_hello_enabled' is not set. Without ECH, the update server hostname is visible in cleartext TLS ClientHello packets, allowing passive observers to map management plane topology, identify update endpoints, and correlate update activity with component identities — even when payload content is encrypted. This enables reconnaissance supporting T1040 (Network Sniffing) and T1048.003.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use OpenSSL or a TLS probe to capture and inspect the ClientHello from the update client to determine whether the SNI field is encrypted.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If ECH is active, SNI will be absent or encrypted in the ClientHello; if disabled, the plaintext hostname appears in the server_name extension.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the TLS library configuration for the update client (e.g., nginx, HAProxy, curl-based agent) for ECH directives. Check for 'ech', 'encrypted_client_hello', or equivalent settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A directive such as 'ssl_ech on;' or 'ech-config-file /path/to/ech.pem' confirms ECH is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture update channel traffic with tcpdump and inspect the TLS handshake to verify whether the SNI field is present in plaintext in the ClientHello message.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i <interface> -w /tmp/update-tls.pcap port <update-server-port> & sleep 10 && kill %1; tshark -r /tmp/update-tls.pcap -Y 'tls.handshake.type == 1' -T fields -e tls.handshake.extensions.server_name
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If ECH is enabled, no plaintext SNI hostname appears in the ClientHello extensions; the field is empty or absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the update agent's management API or health endpoint (if exposed) to retrieve its active TLS configuration including ECH status.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON response containing a field such as 'encrypted_client_hello: true' or 'ech_enabled: true' confirms the feature is active.

option_description: Defines the network accessibility of the configuration update channel endpoint, categorizing it as publicly reachable, internally unrestricted, restricted to a management network, or localhost-only. This determines the attacker population that can reach the channel and informs risk surface calculations for rate-limiting and mTLS requirements.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this attribute in two rules. In 'absence_of_rate_limiting_on_update_channel', exposures are triggered when 'update_channel_exposure' is 'public' or 'internal_unrestricted' and rate limiting is absent, and also when exposure is 'management_network_only' without connection limits. In 'missing_mutual_tls_authentication', exposure scope informs risk weighting. Public or internal_unrestricted channels dramatically expand the attacker population able to flood the channel (T1499.002, T1498) or attempt impersonation without mTLS. Management-network-only or localhost-only values reduce but do not eliminate risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate firewall rules and network policies controlling inbound access to the update channel port to determine which source networks can reach it.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v | grep <update-port>; nft list ruleset | grep <update-port>; ss -tlnp | grep <update-port>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules should show either '0.0.0.0/0' (public), specific internal CIDR ranges (internal_unrestricted or management_network_only), or '127.0.0.1' (localhost_only) as allowed sources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) AuthorizationPolicy, or cloud security group rules governing the update service to identify allowed ingress sources.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -A -o yaml | grep -A20 'ingress' | grep -E 'from|podSelector|namespaceSelector|ipBlock'; kubectl get svc <update-service> -o yaml | grep -E 'type:|loadBalancer'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A NetworkPolicy limiting ingress to a management namespace indicates 'management_network_only'; no NetworkPolicy or an open LoadBalancer service suggests 'public' or 'internal_unrestricted'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the cloud provider's security group or firewall console to review inbound rules for the update channel port.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → EC2 → Security Groups → select the SG attached to the update server → Inbound Rules → filter by update port; or GCP Console → VPC Network → Firewall → filter by target tag and port.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Source CIDR of '0.0.0.0/0' maps to 'public'; a management CIDR block maps to 'management_network_only'; '10.0.0.0/8' without further restriction maps to 'internal_unrestricted'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to connect to the update channel port from hosts on different network segments (external, general internal, management VLAN, localhost) to empirically determine actual reachability.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Successful connection from a public or general internal host indicates broader exposure than 'management_network_only'; failure from all external hosts but success from management VLAN confirms restricted exposure.
